intro: Read the deck for the facts and these notes for the thinking. Each note explains a slide, gives you something to remember and warns you where people slip. Work the section exercises in pencil, answer the recall questions before you check, and use the margins for your own cases.

sections.title: Why Digital Ethics Matters
sections.big_idea: Digital systems carry a promise and a cost together. At national scale **a small failure rate is a population**, so ethics starts at the first design meeting.
in_plain_words: Mobile money, biometric IDs, e-governance and AI have reached deep into the lives of the poor in South Asia, and they did include people the paper system never found. They can also exclude. Because one ruleset serves hundreds of millions, an error repeats everywhere and stays invisible, since a person turned away shows in the dashboard as a transaction that never happened.

Digital ethics is a set of questions asked from the first meeting: who benefits, who is harmed, who can opt out and who decides. The same questions cost an hour at design and a rebuild at launch. Count the failures, and take the **five core questions** to every vendor demonstration.

diagram.note: at this scale a design flaw acts as a policy

key_terms.meaning: How digital tools should be designed, deployed and governed to respect rights, dignity and fairness.
People who depend on a system and cannot walk away from it.
Counting rejections, by shop and by day, so exclusion becomes visible.
A person who can serve someone when the system breaks.

worked_example.title: 99 per cent of a billion
worked_example.setup: A national system works for 99 per cent of a billion people. How many does it fail?
steps: Failure rate = 1 − 0.99 = 0.01.
The deck says these are disproportionately the old, manual labourers and people furthest from a working network.
worked_example.answer: Ten million people, concentrated among those with least power.

mistakes: Treating the promise and the cost as a contest. Both are true at once, and programmes that see only one make predictable mistakes.
Trusting a dashboard that counts transactions. A person turned away appears as nothing at all.
Adding ethics as a launch review, when the cost of changing a design is lowest at the first meeting.

recall.q: Name the five questions to ask of any digital system.
recall.a: Who benefits and who bears the risk; who is excluded; what data is collected and could it be used against people; who decides and can it be contested; what if it breaks.

recall.q: Why is a failure rate a population at national scale?
recall.a: Even 99 per cent success across a billion people leaves ten million failed.

recall.q: What makes exclusion invisible in a dashboard?
recall.a: A turned-away person appears as a transaction that never happened, with no failure recorded.

recall.q: What one practical step makes exclusion visible?
recall.a: Count authentication rejections by shop and by day.

sections.title: Data Privacy & Protection
sections.big_idea: Personal data is anything traceable to a person, alone or combined. **Collect less, bind it to a purpose, and delete it on schedule.**
in_plain_words: Privacy is the power to decide who knows what about you. Puttaswamy (2017) made it a fundamental right under Article 21 and gave a four-step test: legality, legitimate aim, necessity and proportionality. Most programmes fail at necessity, because nobody asked what they would do if they could not collect the data.

Consent must be free, informed, specific and revocable, and purpose limitation and minimisation follow from it. The DPDP Act, 2023 applies to NGOs of every size. Removing names gives weak protection, since village, age, caste and occupation together can identify one person.

diagram.caption: a restriction on privacy must clear every step

key_terms.meaning: Information relating to an identifiable person, alone or in combination with other fields.
The Puttaswamy test that an intrusion be lawful, necessary and proportionate.
Data collected for one purpose should not be reused for another.
A field such as age or village that identifies a person in combination.
Collecting the least you need.

worked_example.title: Run the test on a GPS field
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: an NGO plans to collect each household's precise GPS location. Apply the four steps.
steps: Legality: is the collection backed by a law, or only by a circular? Check this first.
Legitimate aim: the aim, such as reaching families, may be real, but ask whether it is stated so broadly it justifies anything.
Necessity: the deck says village or block is usually enough, so a less intrusive option exists.
Proportionality: put a number on the benefit and describe the harm to the excluded in the same terms.
worked_example.answer: Precise GPS fails the necessity step, so collect the village or block.

mistakes: Believing that dropping names makes a dataset anonymous. Combinations of quasi-identifiers still identify people in small areas.
Reading 'we are a small NGO' as an exemption from the DPDP Act. Obligations scale with what you process.
Calling a thumbprint on an unexplained form consent, when consent has to be free and informed.
Setting a retention period later. Nobody does, because someone can always imagine a use.

recall.q: Which article did Puttaswamy (2017) read privacy into?
recall.a: Article 21, the right to life and liberty.

recall.q: Name the four steps of the proportionality test.
recall.a: Legality, legitimate aim, necessity and proportionality.

recall.q: Which step decides most real cases?
recall.a: Necessity: whether a less intrusive means was considered.

recall.q: What four properties must consent have?
recall.a: It must be free, informed, specific and revocable.

recall.q: Name two ways to reduce re-identification risk.
recall.a: Coarsen quasi-identifiers or aggregate before release, or restrict access.

sections.title: Algorithmic Bias & Fairness
sections.big_idea: Bias is inherited from data, proxies and objectives, all human choices. **Aggregate accuracy hides the group that pays**, so audit by group, repeatedly.
in_plain_words: A model learns from records of an unequal world, and gaps in the data are read as facts. A village surveyed rarely looks like a village with little need. Removing caste or gender does not help when surname, pincode or occupation carry the same signal, and a model that gives a group less service produces data that confirms its own bias.

Fairness has several definitions that cannot all hold when base rates differ, so choosing one is a value judgement. Ask which was chosen and by whom. An audit disaggregates error rates, tests for proxies, documents the training data, repeats on a schedule and records who signed off.

diagram.caption: each turn deepens the gap and looks like accuracy

key_terms.meaning: A systematic, unfair difference in how an automated system treats different groups.
A field such as pincode or surname that stands in for a removed trait.
A cycle where the model's output shapes the data it later learns from.
Report performance separately by gender, caste, region and language.
How common an outcome is within a group; when they differ, fairness definitions conflict.

worked_example.title: Unpick a 12 per cent error rate
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: 1,000 people are scored. 200 belong to group B, which has a 26% error rate, and the overall error rate is 12%. What is the rate for the other 800?
steps: Total errors = 1,000 × 0.12 = 120.
Errors in group B = 200 × 0.26 = 52.
Errors in the other group = 120 − 52 = 68.
Their error rate = 68 ÷ 800 = 0.085, or 8.5%.
worked_example.answer: 8.5% against 26%: the overall 12% hides a gap of more than three to one.

mistakes: Treating the algorithm as neutral. Someone chose the objective, the data and the threshold.
Saying 'we do not collect caste' as proof of fairness, when proxies can reconstruct it.
Quoting one overall accuracy figure and stopping there.
Auditing once. Populations drift, and a model correct in 2024 is not therefore correct now.

recall.q: Name three sources of bias covered in this section.
recall.a: The training data, proxies for protected traits, and feedback loops.

recall.q: Why can't you fix bias by deleting the caste column?
recall.a: Surname, pincode or occupation can stand in for it, and you lose the ability to check.

recall.q: Why can't every fairness definition hold at once?
recall.a: When base rates differ between groups they conflict, which is mathematically proved.

recall.q: What should an audit ask for first?
recall.a: Error rates by gender, caste, region and language.

recall.q: How do you break a feedback loop?
recall.a: Reserve a share of outreach where the model says not to, as a written rule.

sections.title: AI in Development
sections.big_idea: AI magnifies whatever it is given. **Match human oversight to the cost of being wrong**, and keep a person accountable and reachable.
in_plain_words: AI can translate, screen scans, find likely-eligible households and triage reports, extending reach where services never went. It also brings opacity, automated exclusion and confident wrong answers. A false 'ineligible' is noticed only by the person excluded, while a false 'eligible' is noticed by auditors, so incentives push thresholds toward excluding more people.

The safeguard for rights and entitlements is a human in the loop: AI suggests, a human reviews and decides, and the affected person can question the decision. Oversight scales with stakes, from editing a draft to a clinician confirming every scan. Put the pre-pilot questions in writing before the pilot starts.

key_terms.meaning: A system whose reasoning cannot be inspected or explained.
A confident, fluent answer from generative AI that is simply wrong.
A person who reviews, decides and is accountable for an AI-informed decision.
A wrongly excluded person, noticed only by the person excluded.
A tool built for low-stakes use later informs a high-stakes decision.

worked_example.title: Set the guardrail by stakes
worked_example.setup: Four proposed uses of AI arrive in one meeting. Give each a stakes level and a guardrail.
steps: Draft a report summary: low stakes, so a human edits before sending.
Translate a notice: medium stakes, so a native speaker verifies it.
Screen a medical scan: high stakes, so a clinician confirms every case.
Decide benefit eligibility: very high stakes, so a human decides and an appeal route stays open.
worked_example.answer: Low, medium, high and very high, with a stronger guardrail at each step.

mistakes: Calling a tool advisory when overriding it needs justification and accepting it does not. It then decides in practice.
Judging a pilot by its result. Pilots run with the vendor present, on the best sites, with staff trained last week.
Trusting fluent output in a language your team cannot read.
Letting a drafting tool become the basis for decisions without revisiting its guardrail.

recall.q: Name two things AI can do well in development, per the deck.
recall.a: Any two of translation, diagnostics, targeting and triage.

recall.q: Why is a wrongful exclusion invisible?
recall.a: Only the excluded person notices it, and they usually stop coming.

recall.q: What are the four steps of human-in-the-loop?
recall.a: AI suggests, a human reviews, a human decides and is accountable, the affected person can question it.

recall.q: What does 'explainable' have to mean?
recall.a: Understandable to the affected person, specific, actionable and available before the appeal deadline.

recall.q: What question exposes an advisory tool that really decides?
recall.a: What share of suggestions were overridden last quarter?

sections.title: Digital Identity & Inclusion
sections.big_idea: A digital ID gives the invisible a way in and gives the machine a way to turn people away. **Judge it by its failure cases**, and build a manual fallback.
in_plain_words: UIDAI had generated 145.32 crore Aadhaar numbers by 28 September 2026. The gains are real: a portable identity for people with no documents, bank accounts for women in their own names, and some removal of duplicates. The harms are real too, and they fall on the intended beneficiaries: worn fingerprints, weak networks, downtime and no linked mobile for the OTP fallback.

Aadhaar is optional to obtain under s3, yet government may require it for subsidies under s7, which the Supreme Court upheld in 2018. So ask what happens to someone who says no. Replace flattering metrics such as enrolment with tests: authentication success by district and age, failed attempts, and eligible people removed.

right.title: Harms
items: Function creep and no real opt-out

key_terms.meaning: A 12-digit number linked to fingerprints, iris scans and a photograph.
The statutory authority that runs Aadhaar.
A biometric or network mismatch that blocks an entitled person.
A log where a dealer records a manual issue when authentication fails.
Consent given because refusal means losing a basic service.

worked_example.title: An average that hides a district
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: District A had 4,000 authentication attempts and 3,920 succeeded. District B had 1,000 attempts and 900 succeeded.
steps: District A failures = 4,000 − 3,920 = 80, and 80 ÷ 4,000 = 0.02.
District B failures = 1,000 − 900 = 100, and 100 ÷ 1,000 = 0.1.
Combined attempts = 4,000 + 1,000 = 5,000, and combined failures = 80 + 100 = 180.
Combined failure rate = 180 ÷ 5,000 = 0.036.
worked_example.answer: 3.6% overall, which hides 10% in District B. Report by district.

mistakes: Overstating what Aadhaar holds or is. Critiques that overstate are easy to dismiss and take the sound objections down with them.
Conceding nothing to the gains. For the undocumented, a verifiable identity is a real expansion of what they can do.
Building a fallback that counts against the dealer. A route nobody dares use exists only on paper.
Requiring an ID number in your own programme when the service does not need it.

recall.q: How many Aadhaar numbers had UIDAI generated by 28 September 2026?
recall.a: 145.32 crore.

recall.q: Which section lets government require Aadhaar for subsidies?
recall.a: Section 7 of the Aadhaar Act, upheld by the Supreme Court in 2018.

recall.q: Name two authentication failure modes.
recall.a: Any two of worn fingerprints, no connectivity, downtime, demographic mismatch, no linked mobile.

recall.q: What are the four steps of the fallback path?
recall.a: Biometric fails, try an alternative, still fails and log a manual exception, entitlement delivered.

recall.q: Name one metric that tests a system.
recall.a: Authentication success rate by district and by age.

sections.title: Surveillance, Power & Consent
sections.big_idea: Delivery systems produce surveillance as a by-product. **Asymmetry of visibility and power**, more than any technology, is the ethical fault line.
in_plain_words: Ration records show where a person was, attendance shows movement and association, health registers show conditions, and grievance portals show who complained about whom. Each is defensible alone. Joined on one identifier they become a profile. Function creep follows from a series of reasonable requests, and the data outlives the promise made at collection.

The poor are watched most: biometrics at every transaction, weekly location, justification for any change. Conditions sort people by capacity to comply, and belief that a record exists is enough to make someone skip a clinic or a complaint. Guardrails must be built into the system: deletion dates, separate databases, logged joins and independent oversight.

key_terms.meaning: Data gathered for one purpose gradually used for others, without fresh consent.
Self-censorship caused by the suspicion of being monitored.
Aid made conditional on monitored behaviour.
Joining datasets on a common identifier to build one profile.
They can see you and you cannot see them.

worked_example.title: Four guards on an attendance record
worked_example.setup: An NGO keeps a biometric attendance record for a feeding programme. Apply the four guards against function creep.
steps: Bind the purpose in writing: attendance for the programme, with a new basis required for any new use.
Set a deletion date at collection, since retention is never set later.
Separate the identifier: hold service data and identity data apart, joinable only under a rule.
Log every access: who read a record, when and why.
worked_example.answer: A record with a stated purpose, a deletion date, a separated key and an access log.

mistakes: Asking whether there is a camera. The deck says the question is who can see, link and act on the data, and whether the watched person can say no.
Treating each dataset as harmless because each is defensible alone.
Offering a grievance channel that needs the capability the grievance is about.
Making a promise in a memo. An undocumented promise is not a control.

recall.q: What turns four service records into one profile?
recall.a: Joining them on a common identifier.

recall.q: Name the four guards against function creep.
recall.a: Bind the purpose, set a deletion date, separate the identifier and log every access.

recall.q: What is a chilling effect?
recall.a: Self-censorship caused by suspecting a record might be kept and used.

recall.q: Why is consent weak in an NGO programme?
recall.a: Refusal may be read as ingratitude or disqualification, and the asker often decides help.

recall.q: Why must safeguards be built into the system?
recall.a: Built-in controls survive a change of management; intentions do not.

sections.title: The Digital Divide
sections.big_idea: The divide has many levels, from owning a device to using it for something that matters. **Measure at the top level**, and keep an offline route funded.
in_plain_words: A household phone counts as access for everyone in the home, yet a device you control often fails for women and younger members. After the device come affordable data, skills and language, and then meaningful use. Five axes can stack on one person: income, language, literacy, disability and age.

Most inclusion funding sits at levels one and two, where progress is countable, while most benefit sits at level four. Digital-by-default becomes digital-or-nothing once the counter closes. Many people depend on an intermediary and share OTPs, so design delegated access. Voice (IVR) is the cheapest high-value fix.

diagram.caption: closing the first level leaves three to go

key_terms.meaning: Unequal access to devices, connectivity, skills and meaningful use.
A service moved online, which can become digital-or-nothing.
A relative, shopkeeper or kiosk operator who helps someone use a service.
A voice route covering literacy, language and low-end devices together.
Using a device for something that improves your life.

worked_example.title: Which level does each fix reach?
worked_example.setup: A funder lists four interventions. Place each at its level and say what it leaves unsolved.
steps: Distribute devices and build towers: level 1, access. Cost of use, skills and relevance remain.
Subsidised data: level 2, affordability. Skills, language and relevance remain.
Digital literacy training: level 3, skills. Whether anything useful is there remains.
Services worth using, in the right language: level 4, meaningful use, which is the point of the other three.
worked_example.answer: Levels 1, 2, 3 and 4, with only the last measuring whether the rest mattered.

mistakes: Counting household phone ownership as access for every member of the household.
Reporting devices distributed as an outcome. It is an input.
Fixing one axis, such as language, and expecting usage to move for someone facing all five.
Letting the offline route be permitted on paper while it is unfunded, unstaffed and unadvertised.

recall.q: Name the four layers of the digital divide.
recall.a: Access, affordability, skills and language, and meaningful use.

recall.q: Why does household phone ownership mislead?
recall.a: It hides who in the household controls the device.

recall.q: What is the cheapest high-value fix named?
recall.a: Voice, such as an IVR path.

recall.q: What must stay true of an offline route?
recall.a: It must remain funded, staffed and advertised.

recall.q: What does an assisted-use design need?
recall.a: Delegated access with its own credential, a visible record and limits on helpers.

sections.title: Platform Power & Data Colonialism
sections.big_idea: A few firms own the rails, and value flows one way. **Use platforms with an exit that exists**: your own copy of data, in an open format.
in_plain_words: Operating systems, app stores, search, cloud, payments and identity sit with a handful of firms, mostly headquartered abroad, so the rules reach you through a support queue. Data colonialism is a metaphor with limits: data is not depleted by being taken and users do get a service. The observation still stands that value flows from the producers to firms elsewhere, and 'free' is paid for in data.

NGOs build on rented rails such as a messaging app, a cloud provider or an ad platform, and one rule change can end outreach overnight. Two cheap mitigations cover most of the risk: scheduled exports in an open format, and a manual process that could run for a fortnight. Test sovereignty by agency, because moving data home changes who holds it and may leave the person with no say.

diagram.caption: the producers rarely own it or shape the terms

key_terms.meaning: Large-scale extraction of data from the Global South for the benefit of firms elsewhere.
Platforms you build on but do not control.
Meaningful control by a community or country over data about its people.
Dependence that makes leaving a platform too costly.
A data format you could move to another system.

worked_example.title: A dependency check
worked_example.setup: An NGO recruits through an ad platform, delivers by a messaging app and holds records with a cloud provider. For each, ask what a change would do.
steps: Messaging app: a policy change ends your outreach, without notice.
Cloud provider: a pricing change or account action freezes operations.
Ad platform: a category ban removes your reach overnight.
Mitigate with the two cheap steps: keep your own copy of essential data in an open format, and know the manual process that could run for a fortnight.
worked_example.answer: Three single points of failure, softened by an open-format copy and a manual fallback.

mistakes: Using the colonial metaphor without its limits. Stating them is what keeps it from becoming a slogan.
Assuming local storage protects people. A domestic state can be the more immediate risk.
Advising refusal of platforms your participants already use. Nobody can act on that.
Asking participants to reach you through a platform without knowing its data terms.

recall.q: Name the four layers where a few firms act as gatekeepers.
recall.a: Operating system and app store, search and feed ranking, cloud hosting, and payments and identity.

recall.q: Give one place the colonialism analogy strains.
recall.a: Data is not depleted by being taken, and users receive a real service.

recall.q: What are the two cheap mitigations for dependence?
recall.a: Keep your own copy of data in an open format, and know a manual process for a fortnight.

recall.q: What is the better test of sovereignty than location?
recall.a: Agency: can the people described set terms, see what is held and refuse?

sections.title: Misinformation & Online Harms
sections.big_idea: Falsehood travels on trust in the messenger. **A trusted person inside the group beats a label** that cannot reach a closed chat.
in_plain_words: Misinformation is false but shared without intent to harm, and disinformation is deliberate. Inside a closed group a message carries the sender's credibility, with no like-count or correction, and encryption hides its origin. False child-kidnapper messages have been linked to mob killings in India. Scams borrow real processes such as KYC updates and scheme fees.

Moderation is thinnest in the languages with the most users, because investment tracks revenue. Removing content also risks silencing dissent, so ask who decides and who can appeal. What helps: forward limits, prebunking, local fact-checking and, strongest, trusted messengers such as health workers and teachers. Add rumour monitoring to your feedback channels and name someone to reply within a day.

left.title: Misinformation
items: False, shared without intent to harm
Treat the sender as a target to reach

right.title: Disinformation
items: Aims to deceive, profit or incite

key_terms.meaning: False content shared without intent to harm.
False content spread deliberately to deceive, profit or incite.
Teaching the technique before the lie; it generalises but effects decay.
A cap on mass forwarding that cuts velocity without reading content.
A known community voice, the strongest single factor in countering rumour.

worked_example.title: Match the cause to the response
worked_example.setup: Four causes of a rumour turning violent are listed on the deck. Pair each with what has helped.
steps: A rumour circulating faster than any check: forward limits, which cut velocity.
No authoritative account for hours or days: police and administration publishing verified facts early.
A stranger present in an unfamiliar place: local volunteers who can say 'this is not from here'.
Recaptioned footage from elsewhere: reverse image search, taught at community level.
worked_example.answer: Limits, early facts, local volunteers and reverse image search, in that order.

mistakes: Responding to a worried relative as though they ran the campaign. They are a target, and you lose the only channel into the group.
Warning generically. Scams copy legitimate processes, so teach what the real process looks like.
Assuming a platform report will be actioned in an under-resourced language.
Treating moderation as only safety. Over-removal silences dissent and minorities.

recall.q: What separates misinformation from disinformation?
recall.a: Intent: disinformation is spread deliberately.

recall.q: Why does a closed group make a rumour harder to counter?
recall.a: Credibility comes from the sender, and nothing can be labelled or corrected.

recall.q: Name two scams aimed at new users.
recall.a: Any two of fake KYC updates, bogus scheme or lottery fees, loan-app traps, OTP requests.

recall.q: Why is moderation weak in Indian languages?
recall.a: Few reviewers, little classifier data, code-mixing and unmapped slurs, with investment following revenue.

recall.q: What is the strongest single response factor?
recall.a: Trusted community messengers.

sections.title: Responsible Design & Principles
sections.big_idea: Most digital harm is designed in early and found late. **Ask the ethical questions at the first design meeting**, when every fix is still cheap.
in_plain_words: Fields, offline routes, objectives and appeals each cost a conversation at design and a migration, a budget, a retraining or a new institution after launch. Defaults decide outcomes, since few users change them, so the setting you ship is the policy. The cheapest habit is to collect less, using coarse fields such as age bands and blocks.

Do no digital harm means mapping who could be harmed and how data could be misused, naming groups and realistic misusers such as a family member or a local official, building a safeguard into the system itself and signing off the residual risk in writing. Design with people, who know the failure modes, and build redress in from the start.

right.title: After launch
items: Objective: retraining, a year to revisit

key_terms.meaning: Protections built into the design and the defaults from the outset.
The humanitarian principle applied to data and technology.
Risk that remains after safeguards; someone should sign for it.
Involving affected people in design, to find harms before they scale.
A reachable way to contest a decision, with a human who can override.

worked_example.title: Audit a survey form
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a survey form collects four fields. Apply the minimisation table.
steps: Caste: keep only if disaggregation is actually reported; otherwise it is a liability.
Full date of birth: an age band is almost always sufficient.
Precise GPS of a household: village or block is usually enough, and far safer.
Phone number of every member: one contact serves the purpose.
worked_example.answer: Coarsen or drop each field, which removes four ways for the data to be misused.

mistakes: Bolting ethics on at the launch review, when data is collected and exclusions are baked in.
Using a polite misuse case. The realistic one is often a family member or a local official, and rarely a sophisticated attacker.
Running a consultation after the build with hand-picked people. It produces endorsement that then gets cited.
Accepting residual risk without naming who decided and on what basis.

recall.q: Why is ethics at the launch review too late?
recall.a: Data is collected, the model is trained and exclusions are baked in; reversal costs more than anyone spends.

recall.q: Why do defaults matter?
recall.a: Few users change them, so the shipped setting is the policy.

recall.q: Name the four steps of do no digital harm.
recall.a: Map who could be harmed, map misuse, design safeguard and fallback, decide on residual risk.

recall.q: Name one question from the Principles for Digital Development table.
recall.a: For example: who runs this when the grant ends?

recall.q: What makes redress real?
recall.a: A route usable without a smartphone and a human who can override without penalty.

sections.title: Governance, Regulation & Practice
sections.big_idea: Governance has four layers, and the practitioner acts most often. **Put commitments in contracts and schemas**, because assurances leave with the account manager.
in_plain_words: Law sets rights, a regulator can investigate and penalise, an organisation sets policy and a practitioner decides what goes on the form. The Data Protection Board of India handles breaches and grievances. Judge any authority on independence, capacity, power to compel and breadth of remit, and check its current position, since composition and exemptions are still settling.

People hold four rights: access, correction, erasure and grievance. Test whether you could answer an access request tomorrow. Buying a tool is where most ethics is decided, so ask the vendor about storage, bias testing, exit, uptime and liability and put each answer in the contract. The checklist covers purpose, consent, inclusion, bias, security and redress.

levels.label: Practitioner
levels.sub: decides what is on the form

diagram.caption: the last layer acts most often and is trained least

key_terms.meaning: The DPDP Act body for breaches and grievances.
Knowing what data is held about you.
Having data deleted when it is no longer needed.
A third party handling your data for the vendor; ask for the list.
A written commitment that survives a change of account manager.

worked_example.title: Turn vendor answers into clauses
worked_example.setup: You are buying a tool. Pair each question with the contract term the deck suggests.
steps: Where is data stored, and who can access it? Name jurisdictions and list the sub-processors.
Has it been tested for bias and accessibility? Require disaggregated performance, supplied annually.
What happens to our data if we leave? Require export in an open format and certified deletion.
Uptime and liability: agree a manual process for outages and write a liability clause.
worked_example.answer: Four questions, four clauses. A verbal assurance is worth nothing once the account manager changes.

mistakes: Assuming the regulator will notice a small deployment. The deck says most small deployments are out of its reach.
Treating compliance as an annual review, when the practitioner makes hundreds of small decisions a year.
Relying on a verbal assurance from a vendor instead of a clause.
Teaching your community nothing about their rights. A right nobody knows about protects nobody.

recall.q: Name the four layers of governance.
recall.a: Law, regulator, organisation and practitioner.

recall.q: What four rights does the deck list?
recall.a: Access, correction, erasure and grievance.

recall.q: What three things make an authority effective?
recall.a: Independence, adequate capacity, and power to compel and penalise (plus a broad remit).

recall.q: Name the six checklist areas.
recall.a: Purpose, consent, inclusion, bias, security and redress.

recall.q: Which course should you read first if you read one book?
recall.a: Eubanks, Automating Inequality, for its welfare cases.

notes.2: Use the agenda as a map of the argument. Sections 2 to 4 describe harms in data and algorithms, 5 to 9 cover identity, surveillance, the divide, platforms and misinformation, and 10 and 11 give the response. If one decision is pending, jump to **Section 11**.
notes.4: Read the table row by row, because each promise has a matching failure. The aim is to **hold gain and cost together**. Memorise the scale line: 99 per cent success across a billion people still fails ten million, and they live furthest from the network.
notes.5: Underline 'least power to refuse'. A pensioner cannot walk away the way a shopper can, so the same design is judged more strictly. The table shows the price of timing: the same questions cost **an hour at design and a rebuild at launch**.
notes.6: The fourth row matters most. A person turned away appears in the dashboard as a transaction that never happened, so **the system reports success while excluding people**. Your practical move is cheap engineering: count authentication rejections by shop and by day.
notes.7: Use the second table as a cross-examination tool: when someone claims a benefit, ask the matching question. 'It cuts leakage' is the sharpest, because removing ghosts and removing eligible people look **identical in the headline beneficiary count**.
notes.8: Scale turns a design choice into a policy. One ruleset means errors replicate, and designing out discretion removes the clerk who could fix a widow's name spelled two ways. Keep the closing point too: **one fix also propagates to everyone**, so a good exception route protects millions.
notes.9: Place yourself in both columns. As a deployer you choose fields, retention, offline routes and exports, and that is where your real power sits. As a user of other systems, **document failures with counts and dates**, because documented exclusion is what eventually changes a national system.
notes.10: Memorise these five and carry them into any vendor demo. Every bad answer in the table is true and still dodges the question, because it describes **the average case when you asked about the failing case**. None of the questions needs technical vocabulary.
notes.11: The table promises five abilities, each tied to a section. Pick the row that matches your job and read that section first. The deck uses South Asian examples because **assumptions about consent, opting out and regulators hold differently here** than in European or American material.
notes.13: Personal data is anything traceable to a person, alone or combined. The village row shows it: a village is thousands of people, yet village plus two more fields may be one household. Judge **minimisation across the whole record**, and take most care in small hamlets.
notes.14: The 'nothing to hide' argument fails in four ways, listed in the table. Remember the second row best: **data outlives the law that allowed it**. Design as if the least trustworthy plausible future custodian will hold your database, because eventually one will.
notes.15: Puttaswamy is your anchor case: nine judges held privacy a fundamental right under Article 21. Use it in internal arguments, since 'is this **necessary and proportionate**?' is a constitutional standard and asking it shifts who must justify. The judgment supplies a test and no one to apply it.
notes.16: Learn the four steps as a sequence: legality, legitimate aim, necessity, proportionality. Most real cases turn on step three, so ask 'what would we do if we could not collect this?' At step four **put a number on both sides**, including the harm to the excluded.
notes.17: Check the four tests: free, informed, specific, revocable. The sharpest is 'free', because consent given to keep a pension is not free however good the form. Try the closing test on your own work: **if nobody declined last year, you were collecting signatures**.
notes.18: Two separate rules. Purpose limitation says immunisation records are not a recruitment list, and minimisation says every extra field is a future liability. The grievance row is where NGOs slip most: identifiable complaints without access rules form **a list of people who spoke up**. Set deletion dates at collection.
notes.19: Treat this slide as orientation. Being a small NGO gives no exemption, and obligations track what you process. Work down the table: write the purpose of each field, name your basis per dataset, name a person for requests, and know whom you would tell after a breach. **Check current rules** before relying on it.
notes.20: Deleting names is the weakest step. The real risk is a combination of quasi-identifiers such as age, place and caste, especially in small areas. Work down the table from coarsening to aggregating to **restricting access**, the option most often skipped. Releasing at district level usually costs little detail you need.
notes.22: Algorithms optimise whatever people hand them. The table lists four human choices: what to predict, what data to use, what counts as success, where to put the threshold. When someone says 'the algorithm decided', ask **who chose the objective**. There is always a person.
notes.23: Bias is a systematic unfair difference in outcomes between groups, and it is usually inherited. Every row in the table has one shape: an under-served group produced thin data, and the model read the absence as a trait of the group. In the fraud row, **the model learns who was investigated**.
notes.24: This is bias source one. Missing data means 'not recorded', yet a model treats it as 'not there'. Read the table as pairs of gap and wrong conclusion. The practical safeguard is **a written note of who is missing from the training set**, made at collection time because it cannot be rebuilt later.
notes.25: Source two is proxies. Removing a sensitive column does not stop a model finding surname, pincode or occupation. 'We do not collect caste' therefore proves nothing about fairness. The usual resolution is to **hold caste data separately for audit only** and never show it to the model.
notes.26: Trace the loop on the diagram: biased data, a low score, less service, new data that confirms the bias. It feels like accuracy because the model causes the outcomes it predicts. To break it you must **reserve a share of outreach where the model says not to**, as a written rule.
notes.27: Read the chart as an illustration; it contains no real data. The lesson is the arithmetic of averages: a 12% overall error can hide 26% for one group. Whenever a vendor quotes one accuracy figure, ask for **the same figure split by group**.
notes.28: Fairness has several definitions: equal selection rates, equal error rates, equal precision. When base rates differ they cannot all hold, a mathematical result that no engineering effort removes. So ask for **disclosure**: which definition, chosen by whom, and whether affected people had a say. That belongs in procurement.
notes.29: Use the five audit steps as a contract checklist: disaggregate, test for proxies, document the data, re-audit on schedule, record decisions. A model correct in 2024 may be wrong now. **Require disaggregated performance before signing**, since afterwards it is only a favour.
notes.31: AI magnifies whatever it is given, good design or exclusion alike. Before any pilot settle the four questions in the table: advising or deciding, who is accountable, tested on our population, and what the fallback is. Remember the pilot trap: **vendor present, best sites, freshly trained staff**.
notes.32: Four uses to remember: translation, diagnostics, targeting and triage. The slide frames them as help for stretched human workers. Keep that as a test for any proposal: **is the AI extending a person's reach, or standing in for the person?** The next slides cover the risks.
notes.33: A black box gives output without reasons, so the affected person cannot contest it. The table says what 'explainable' must mean: said aloud by a field officer, specific, actionable and **in time for the appeal**. Where entitlements are at stake, a simpler rule that fits one page may serve people better.
notes.34: Compare the two error rows. A wrongly included person is spotted by auditors, while a wrongly excluded person is noticed only by themselves, and they stop coming. Every incentive therefore pushes thresholds toward exclusion. **Count the invisible error** by auditing rejections and surveying dropouts.
notes.35: Fluent text can be wrong text. The danger peaks where the user cannot check: medication, legal sections, scheme eligibility and translation into a language your team cannot read. Keep **a verified human source for high-stakes advice**, and remember the interface gives no meaningful signal of confidence.
notes.36: Follow the four steps: AI suggests, a human reviews, a human decides and is accountable, and the affected person can question the decision. The rule is short: for rights and entitlements, **AI informs a human and never replaces one**. Check that the person in step three is reachable.
notes.37: Match oversight to stakes: edit drafts, verify translations, confirm every scan, and let a human decide eligibility with an appeal open. Calibration is the skill, since oversight nobody follows protects nobody. Watch for **stakes creeping upward** when a drafting tool starts informing decisions.
notes.38: Use these five as a written gate before a pilot. The first row hides the commonest failure: a tool called advisory becomes decisive when overriding it needs a justification. Ask what share of suggestions were **overridden last quarter**; the slide says the answer is usually close to zero.
notes.40: Keep the facts straight, because critiques that overstate the system are easy to dismiss. The table separates what Aadhaar is from what people assume. The fourth row carries the ethics: optional to obtain, yet the state may require it for subsidies. **Cite the section numbers** when you argue.
notes.41: The chart is an illustrative trajectory, and only the end point is real: UIDAI's figure of 145.32 crore numbers generated by 28 September 2026. Use it to remember scale. At this size **a small failure rate means millions of people**.
notes.42: Concede the gains, because dismissing them makes your critique sound ideological. The table names who gains most: people with no documents, women opening their own accounts, migrants and the previously invisible. Then note the last line: an identity that opens access also **gates** everything, which sets up the next slide.
notes.43: Work down the failure table and ask who each row hits. Worn prints hit labourers, weak networks hit remote villages, outages hit a whole district and OTP fallbacks hit women without phones. Failures **concentrate on the intended beneficiaries**. Treat the mechanism as established and the national magnitude as contested.
notes.44: This is a one-slide summary of the dilemma: four dimensions, each with a benefit and a harm. The lesson is stated plainly. Do not reject digital ID; **design for the person the machine fails**. Use it to open a discussion before the fallback slide.
notes.45: Trace the path on the diagram: biometric fails, try an alternative, still fails, log a manual exception, deliver the entitlement. Fallbacks usually fail through incentives. If using the override counts against the dealer, nobody uses it. **Logging also gives you the exclusion data** nobody otherwise collects.
notes.46: Apply one test to any 'voluntary' system: what happens to someone who says no? The table shows ration, scholarship and wage lost, with the SIM card as the exception where law requires another ID. **Check whether the person at the counter knows that.** Turn the test on your own programme too.
notes.47: Carry this idea into all your work: measure a system by **its failure cases**. The right-hand column gives the tests, such as authentication success by district and age, failed attempts, eligible people removed and outage hours in poor-connectivity blocks. All are computable from data the systems already generate.
notes.49: Delivery systems produce surveillance as a by-product, with nobody intending it. Each row in the table is a service record that leaves a trail. The key question is about linkage: each dataset is defensible alone, but joined on one identifier, **four records become one profile**.
notes.50: Function creep arrives as a series of reasonable requests, each defensible alone. Use the four guards in the table: bind the purpose, set a deletion date at collection, separate the identifier, log every access. The closing rule is the one to remember: **write it into the schema, since a memo binds nobody**.
notes.51: The finding is the asymmetry: the poor give biometrics at every transaction while a wealthy person gives a card once. Use the closing test in design meetings: **would we ask this of someone applying for a business loan?** If the answer is no, ask what the requirement is really for.
notes.52: Conditions sort people by capacity to comply. Read the table for who fails each one: the sick, the undocumented, migrants, the non-literate. These are often the people the programme targets. Notice the last row, a **closed loop**: a grievance channel that demands the very capability the grievance is about.
notes.53: A chilling effect needs no actual watcher, because belief that a record exists is enough. The table lists what people skip: clinic visits, meetings, complaints and seeking help after violence. The counter is specificity. **Tell people what is recorded, who sees it and for how long**, since uncertainty does much of the damage.
notes.54: The fault line is an asymmetry of visibility and power. The left column can link, infer, change rules and decline to explain; the right cannot see, learn, withdraw or contest. Run the diagnostic: list what a system knows about a person and what that person can find out. **The gap is the ethical exposure.**
notes.55: Where refusal costs a livelihood, consent cannot be free. The third and fourth rows concern us directly, because an NGO or researcher often also decides who gets help. Separate the roles where you can, and otherwise **ask for less**. The burden shifts to the system to justify what it takes.
notes.56: Five safeguards, each with a paper version and a working version. The working version is enforced by the system itself: a date in the system, separate databases with no shared key, logged joins, oversight that can stop processing, and a complaint route without a smartphone. **Built-in controls survive a change of management.**
notes.58: The divide has five levels in the table: a household device, a device you control, affordable data, skills and language, and meaningful use. The second row hides in statistics, since a man's phone counts as access for his wife. Distributing devices closes only **row one**.
notes.59: The chart is illustrative, but the slide says the pattern is well documented: women in South Asia are markedly less likely to own a phone or use the internet. Connect it to the previous slide, because household ownership figures **hide who actually controls the device**.
notes.60: This is another illustrative chart, now urban against rural internet use. The sentence to keep is about coverage maps: a tower nearby does not mean an affordable, reliable signal inside a home. When you plan, **ask about the signal inside the household**.
notes.61: Five axes are named: income, language, literacy, disability and age. They stack, so a fix on one axis changes little for someone facing all five. The table also names the cheapest high-value fix, **voice (IVR)**, which covers literacy, language and low-end devices together and rarely gets funded.
notes.62: Use the four levels as a ladder: device and signal, affordability, skills and language, then meaningful use. Funding clusters at levels one and two because progress there is countable. **Measure at level four**, people who completed something they needed. Devices distributed is only an input.
notes.63: Digital-by-default turns into digital-or-nothing when the offline channel is quietly withdrawn: the counter closes, paper forms go out of print, staff are reassigned. The rule to defend is that an essential offline route stays **funded, staffed and advertised**. A route nobody pays for or hears about is closed.
notes.64: Many people reach services through a relative, shopkeeper or kiosk operator. The table gives the bargain: access in exchange for OTPs, disclosure and informal fees. Almost no system is designed for assisted use, so design **delegated access with its own credential, a visible record and limits** on what a helper can do.
notes.65: Five design choices bring in people who are otherwise left out: voice, low-end devices, local languages, accessibility and assisted use. Each helps more people than its target group. The instruction that makes the rest work is **measure who is left out**, because usage figures describe only people your design already fits.
notes.67: Four layers of the stack decide what you can do: operating system and app store, search and feed ranking, cloud hosting, and payments and identity. Each has terms set by someone else. Most of these firms sit abroad, so **rules are set under another country's law** and reach you through a support queue.
notes.68: Data colonialism is a metaphor, and the table lets you test both sides: where the analogy holds and where it strains. State the limits, because that stops it turning into a slogan. The sharpest case is AI training: **models trained on local data and sold back as services**.
notes.69: Read the four steps left to right: users generate data, platforms process it abroad, profiles, ads and models are built, and profit and control stay elsewhere. The takeaway is in the last line: the people who produce the data rarely own it or shape its terms, so **value flows one way**.
notes.70: The region offers scale, detailed behavioural and language data, newer regulation and price-sensitive users. The third row cuts both ways: newer regulation can be better designed, as the DPDP Act shows. The risk is the gap between passing a law and **a regulator able to act**. 'Free' is paid for in data.
notes.71: This two-column slide shows who captures value. Platforms gain advertising revenue, training data and lock-in. Users get a free service for now, little say over terms and no share of the value created. Use it when you explain to colleagues why **'free' has a price** here.
notes.72: Ask before you build: what happens to our beneficiaries if this platform changes its rules, raises its price or closes our account? The table gives four dependencies. Two cheap mitigations cover most of the risk: **keep your own copy of essential data in an open format**, and know the manual process that could run for a fortnight.
notes.73: Sovereignty has several forms: localisation, public digital infrastructure, open source and community control, each with a trade-off in the table. Localisation can make data easier for the local state to reach. Use the slide's better test, **agency**: can the people described set terms, see what is held and refuse?
notes.74: The realistic stance is to use platforms with an exit that exists. The table prices four habits: scheduled exports, reading the terms, choosing portable formats and public infrastructure for critical paths. One carries an obligation: if you ask participants to reach you through a platform, **you have enrolled them in its terms**.
notes.76: Separate the two terms: misinformation is false but shared without intent to harm, disinformation is false and deliberate. The difference decides the response, because a worried relative is a target to reach. The table explains the spread: messages arrive from relatives, in closed groups, with **no visible correction**.
notes.77: Trust in the messenger launders the message: a falsehood from your uncle's group carries his authority. The table contrasts open platforms, where labels and corrections are possible, with closed groups, where none are. The intervention that works is **one competent, well-liked person inside the group who checks things**.
notes.78: Treat this as documented fact: false child-kidnapper messages on messaging apps have been linked to mob killings in India. The table pairs causes with helps, from forward limits to reverse image search. The cheapest one within your reach is to **say something true, early and locally**, even if it is only what you know so far.
notes.79: Scams copy real processes, so generic warnings fail. The table gives the pretext behind each scam: real KYC requests, real schemes, missing formal credit and trained habits of sharing OTPs. Note the loan-app harassment point, where contacting a borrower's phone book hurts women most. Teach **how the real process looks**.
notes.80: Two areas of highest damage appear here: health and democracy. Health falsehoods cost lives during COVID-19, and coordinated falsehoods can distort elections and erode trust in institutions. The slide has no table, so use it as a prompt: **which of your programmes touch these two areas** and need a rumour-response plan?
notes.81: Moderation is weak in the languages with the most users: few reviewers, little training data, code-mixing and unmapped slurs. Investment tracks revenue, and risk follows a different path. Never assume a report will be actioned. **Build a trust-and-safety contact before you need one** and keep a dated record of what you reported.
notes.82: Moderation is a real trade-off. Over-removal silences dissent and minorities, under-removal lets harm spread, and no setting avoids both. Watch for safety framing used against criticism. The questions that matter as much as the rule are **who decides and who can appeal**.
notes.83: Four responses, with evidence and cost. Forward limits slow spread without reading content, prebunking teaches technique but effects decay, local fact-checking is essential yet always second to the rumour, and trusted messengers are the strongest factor. Your asset is **health workers, group leaders and teachers**. Add rumour monitoring to your feedback channels.
notes.85: This table is the argument for the section: every decision is cheap at design and costly after launch. Fields, offline routes, objectives and appeals each move from a conversation to a migration, a budget, a retraining or a new institution. Put the **five questions on the agenda of the first design meeting**.
notes.86: Privacy by design means protective defaults. The slide's observation is that few users change a default, so **the setting you ship is the policy**. Compare each pair in the table: sharing off, retention set at collection, access limited, optional fields that are actually optional. Check who can see your beneficiary database today.
notes.87: The Principles for Digital Development, revised in 2024 into nine, are a sector framework that many donors endorse, so citing them helps in proposals. Their weakness is that they are easy to claim. Use the table's questions: **a specific answerable question is harder to assert falsely than a principle**.
notes.88: Follow four steps: map who could be harmed, map how data could be misused, design the safeguard and fallback, then decide on the residual risk. Be specific. Name groups, and name realistic misusers such as a family member or a local official. The last step needs **a signed, dated decision**.
notes.89: Collect less and keep less. Go through the table and ask of your own form whether each field is used. Coarsening is the underused option: age bands for dates of birth, block for GPS, presence of a condition for a diagnosis. Each field you skip is **a breach that cannot happen**.
notes.90: The affected know the failure modes: who controls the phone, which words get read, when people can attend, what failure costs. A test tells you that something failed and not why. Beware late consultation with hand-picked participants, which yields **endorsement that then gets cited**.
notes.91: Redress has four parts: a route to contest, a human who can override, plain-language notice and an exit. Test each against the right column, for example usable without a smartphone. Appeals also show where the design is wrong, which makes a working grievance channel **the cheapest quality assurance** a programme has.
notes.93: Four layers hold systems to account: law, regulator, organisation and practitioner. The table gives what each can and cannot do. The last layer acts most often and gets the least training. Write **a two-page internal standard**: what is never collected, what is always deleted, and whom to ask.
notes.94: The DPDP Act creates a Data Protection Board of India. Judge any authority on four observable properties: independence, staff and technical capacity, power to compel and penalise, and breadth of remit. The slide warns that composition, powers and exemptions are still settling, so **check the current position** before relying on it.
notes.95: Four rights are listed: access, correction, erasure and grievance. The table gives each as a sentence a person might say. A right nobody knows about protects nobody, so explaining them is work for field organisations. Test yourself: if a participant asked for access tomorrow, **could you answer, and how fast**?
notes.96: This six-row checklist compresses the deck: purpose, consent, inclusion, bias, security and redress. Use it before every deployment and write the answers down. Each row points back to a section, so a weak answer tells you where to reread. **Give each row a named owner**.
notes.97: Most organisations buy tools, so procurement is where most digital ethics gets decided. The table pairs each vendor question with a contract term. A verbal assurance disappears when the account manager changes, while **a contract clause survives** and costs nothing extra to request before signing.
notes.98: Five takeaways and five one-step actions, each inside a programme manager's authority. Pick one action this week from the table: delete a field, ask for disaggregated error rates, build a fallback, set a deletion date, or write down what happens to someone who says no. Individual care **fills the gap** while structures are built.
notes.99: Start with Eubanks if you read one book, since it is built from welfare cases and is hard to wave away in a meeting. The table says what each source is best for, from feedback loops (O'Neil) to power in data (D'Ignazio and Klein). The slide also pairs this deck with three companion courses.
